each.e: From Middle English ech, eche, elche, ilch, from Old English ǣlċ, contraction of ǣġhwelċ. Comparable to aye + alike. By surface analysis, Old English ā + which.
each.g: All; every; qualifying a singular noun, indicating all examples of the thing so named seen as individual or separate items (compare every).

eager.e: From Middle English egre, eger, from Old French aigre, egre (modern French aigre), from Latin ācrus, variant of ācer (“sharp, keen”); see acid, acerb, etc.
eager.g: Desirous; keen to do or obtain something.

eagerly.e: From Middle English egrely, egerly; equivalent to eager + -ly.

eagerness.e: From Middle English egernesse, egrenesse; equivalent to eager + -ness.
eagerness.g: The state or quality of being eager; ardent desire.

eagle.e: From Middle English egle, from Anglo-Norman egle, from Old French aigle, from Latin aquila.
eagle.g: Any of several large carnivorous and carrion-eating birds in the family Accipitridae, having a powerful hooked bill and keen vision.

ear.e: From Middle English eare, eere, ere, eyr, ire, yere, ȝhere, from Old English ēare (“ear”), from Proto-West Germanic *auʀā, from the voiced Verner alternant of Proto-Germanic *ausô (“ear”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ṓws (“ear”), from *h₂ew- (“to perceive”).
ear.g: The organ of hearing, consisting of the pinna or auricle, auditory canal, eardrum, malleus, incus, stapes and cochlea.

ear.e: From Middle English eren, from Old English erian, from Proto-West Germanic *arjan, from Proto-Germanic *arjaną, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂erh₃- (“to plough”).

early.e: From Middle English erly, erlich, earlich, from Old English ǣrlīċ (“early”, adjective), equivalent to ere + -ly.
early.g: At a time in advance of the usual or expected event.

early.e: From Middle English erly, orely, arely, erliche, arliche, from Old English ǣrlīċe, ārlīċe (“early; early in the morning”, adverb), equivalent to ere + -ly.
early.g: At a time before expected; sooner than usual.

earn.e: From Middle English ernen, from Old English earnian, from Proto-West Germanic *aʀanōn, from Proto-Germanic *azanōną. This verb is denominal from the noun *azaniz (“harvest”).
earn.g: To gain (success, reward, recognition) through applied effort or work.

earn.e: Probably either: from Middle English erne, ernen (“to coagulate, congeal”) (chiefly South Midlands), a metathetic variant of rennen (“to run; to coagulate, congeal”), from Old English rinnan (“to run”) (with the variants iernan, irnan) and Old Norse rinna (“to move quickly, run; of liquid: to flow, run.
earn.g: To curdle (milk), especially in the cheesemaking process.

earnest.e: From Middle English ernest, eornest, from Old English eornest, eornost, eornust (“earnestness, zeal, seriousness, battle”), from Proto-Germanic *ernustuz (“earnest, strength, solidity, struggle, fight”), a derivative of Proto-Germanic *arniz (“efficient, capable, diligent, sure”), from Proto-Indo-European *er- (“to cause to move, arouse, increase”).

earnest.g: A sum of money paid in advance as a deposit; hence, a pledge, a guarantee, an indication of something to come.

earnestly.e: From Middle English ernestly, from Old English eornostlīċe (“earnestly, strictly”), equivalent to earnest + -ly.
earnestly.g: In an earnest manner; being very sincere; putting forth genuine effort.

earring.e: From Middle English erering, from Old English ēarhring (“ear-ring”), from Proto-West Germanic *auʀahring, equivalent to ear + ring.
earring.g: A piece of jewelry worn on the ear.

earth.e: From Middle English erthe, from Old English eorþe, from Proto-West Germanic *erþu, from Proto-Germanic *erþō (“dirt, ground, earth”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁érteh₂ (“earth”).

earthen.e: From Middle English erthen, urthen, from Old English eorþen, yrþen, ierþen (“made of earth”), from Proto-Germanic *irþīnaz. By surface analysis, earth + -en (“made of”).

earthen.g: to provide or add soil to

earthly.e: From Middle English erthely, erthlich, ierðlich, from Old English eorþlīċ, corresponding to earth + -ly.
earthly.g: Relating to the earth or this world, as opposed to heaven or the heavens.

earthquake.e: From Middle English erthequake, corresponding to earth + quake.
earthquake.g: A shaking of the ground, caused by volcanic activity or movement around geologic faults.

earthy.e: From Middle English erthy, equivalent to earth + -y.

ease.e: From Middle English ese, eise, aise, from Anglo-Norman ese (“ease”), from Old French eise, aise (“elbow room; opportunity”), of uncertain and obscure origin. Apparently related to Provençal ais, Italian agio and asio, Sicilian aciu and Portuguese azo.
ease.g: Lack of difficulty; the ability to do something easily.

easily.e: From Middle English esiliche, equivalent to easy + -ly.

east.e: From Middle English est, from Old English ēast, from Proto-West Germanic *austr, from Proto-Germanic *austrą, from Proto-Germanic *austraz, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂éwsteros (“east”).
east.g: The direction of the earth's rotation, specifically 90°.

eastern.e: From Middle English esturne, esterne, from Old English ēasterne (“eastern”), from Proto-Germanic *austrōnijaz (“eastern”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ews-ro- (“eastern”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ews- (“dawn, east”). Morphologically east + -ern.
eastern.g: Of, facing, situated in, or related to the east.

eastward.e: From Middle English estward, from Old English ēastweard, ēasteweard; equivalent to east + -ward.
eastward.g: The direction or area lying to the east.

easy.e: From Middle English esy, eesy, partly from Middle English ese (“ease”) + -y, equivalent to ease + -y, and partly from Anglo-Norman eisé from Old French aisié (“eased, at ease, at leisure”), past participle of aisier (“to put at ease”), from aise (“empty space, elbow room, opportunity”), of uncertain origin.

eat.e: From Middle English eten, from Old English etan (“to eat”), from Proto-West Germanic *etan, from Proto-Germanic *etaną (“to eat”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁édti, from *h₁ed- (“to eat”).
From Middle English ete, ate, æte, from Old English ǣt (“food, eating”), from Proto-West Germanic *āt, from Proto-Germanic *ētą (“food, thing to eat”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁ed- (“to eat”).
eat.g: Something to be eaten; a meal; a food item.

eaten.e: From Middle English eten, from Old English eten, from Proto-West Germanic *etan, from Proto-Germanic *etanaz; morphologically eat + -en.

eater.e: From Middle English eter, etere, etter, from Old English etere; equivalent to eat + -er (agent noun suffix) or + -er (patient suffix) (food suitable for eating).
eater.g: A person or animal who eats.

eating.e: From Middle English etynge, from Old English eting.

eaves.e: From eave + -s, from a misinterpretation of the -s ending of eaves as forming a plural.
